meaningMnemonic: This is the radical for bear , because it looks like the letter B — B for bear! You know this one is "bear" and not "building" because it's all boxy, like a stocky, chunky bear who's all fat and ready to hibernate.
You have the radical twenty and the kanji one. Put those together and you get 21. What's another name for 21? That's blackjack .

This is a ceremony radical with a slide radical. Why would a ceremony need a slide? For drunkard s, of course! People love to drink at ceremonies, and when they've had too much, those drunkards like to go down slides. If your ceremony has a slide, the drunkards will be happy.
Remember the stairs ( 乃 ) radical? This is a lot like that, but it has another stroke to motorize it. The extra bit makes the stairs move by themselves — that's why this is an escalator !

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means few . Here's a mnemonic refresher, just in case: You have a small slide. The thing about small slides is that few people can use them. Not everyone can fit their bum in a small slide — only a few small ones can make it down. That's why this means "few"!

This radical is the same as the kanji you learned earlier, but the meaning is a little different. It's not just for saying things humbly, it's for being humble in general. When you see this radical, think about being humble. You can kinda see this as someone with their hands pressed together in front of their body, in a very humble posture. Maybe a humble Buddhist monk wearing some big robes? Imagine him all humble there, head bowed, hands pressed together.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means older brother . In case you need a refresher, here's the mnemonic again: Who's someone who's just a mouth with legs? That's your know-it-all older brother, who won't shut up about anything.

This radical means orders , because it looks like Napoleon with his big bicorne hat, giving orders. You move, or his orders move you. See how his body looks like the stamp radical ( 卩 )? If it helps, you can think of Napoleon's written orders as bearing his stamp of approval. All official orders need the stamp of that guy under the big hat, you know?

At first glance, this looks like the Spirit radical, but it's actually just a guy in a similar outfit . You can tell because of that thing sticking off of his sleeve on the right side — that's the outfit's price tag. Where in the world did this guy go to buy an outfit like this?

Imagine a root vegetable, like a turnip or something. See the twisted bulb at the top, with long, stringy root tendrils dangling under it? That's why this is the root radical. Alternatively, focus on the components: sun and kick. When the sun is out, you're outside kicking things around. But be careful — kick a root, and you might trip over it!
This the radical for simple . Why? Because it looks like a simple little stick figure drawing! Just a big head on top with a few hairs, and a stick figure body. What could be more simple?

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means skin . Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: You go down a slide made of branches and your skin scrapes right off — ouch! Lucky for you, it was just your old outer layer of skin, and now you've got a fresh shiny layer. Yay for exfoliation! You're not sure what to do with this big, floppy layer of old skin, though…

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means sound . You can even see someone standing at a kind of square table here. It's a DJ at the turntables! Imagine them spinning records and scratching out all kinds of cool sounds. You could also remember this with the kanji mnemonic we gave you. Here's the gist of it: If you stand on the sun, you'll hear a very loud sizzling sound.

There's a lid on top of something you're trying to keep private. It's your trash . You wouldn't want people going through your private trash, which is why we put lids on our trash cans. It's also illegal to look through someone's trash, so make sure you never do that.

Using your construction power you build something great. A true achievement built for the achievement of making kanji learning easier! Hints Just constructing this thing was an achievement. Feel proud like it was, well, an achievement.
readingMnemonic: This achievement was made possible by こう いち , so of course this construction project is a giant statue of the man himself. What an achievement of a statue. What an achievement of an achievement. Hints Thanks こういち . Now everyone will know of your achievements around kanji learning and inside-out earth theory. Hint: When you see 工 in a kanji it will often take the こう reading. Remember that, because it comes up quite a bit!

meaningMnemonic: After being thrown in prison , a drunkard thinks, "What have I become ?" It's then they resolve to become a better person. Hints Imagine yourself waking up drunk in prison, cold and confused, with a pounding headache. Say out loud: "Is this really what I wanted to become?" As soon as you get out of here, you're going to become a better person. Yeah, cheers to that!
readingMnemonic: Determined to become a better human, you take up a sa ber ( せい ). With this saber in hand, you'll turn your life around and become a new person… a hero… an ally of justice! Hints Feel your fingers tighten around the saber's grip as the desire to become a better person wells up within you. No more drunken prison stints for you — you're going to become someone kids can look up to! You just need a little liquid courage first…

meaningMnemonic: Stand on your older brother . Now stand on your older brother again. You wish to stand on, and above, your older brother. You compete over and over again, to stand atop your older brother. Hints Imagine yourself standing on your older brother. They push you off. So you do it again. You want to be on top, but your older brother doesn't want you to. You compete for the top spot over and over again, throughout your whole life, because that's what one does with their older brother.
readingMnemonic: You compete with your older brother because only one of you may go to きょう と . Whoever stands on top the most gets to go to きょうと , so you must compete for a spot. Hints Imagine yourself competing to stand on top of your older brother. Do you win? Do you get the one ticket to きょうと ?

meaningMnemonic: In prison , Wolverine gets picked on for the barb s coming out of his hands. This creates a lot of conflict between him and the other prisoners. They don't take kindly to mutants, and Wolverine doesn't take kindly to bigots — hence the conflict. Hints Picture one Wolverine versus, like, a hundred prisoners. Who would win? Yeah, my money's on the mutant in this conflict.
readingMnemonic: This constant conflict between Wolverine and the other inmates is really affecting his sou l ( そう ). Despite what people think, Wolverine really doesn't like to fight. He just hates injustice so much, he feels he has to do something about it. Hints Put yourself in Wolverine's shoes. Imagine what it would feel like to have conflicting values, what it would do to your soul. Wanting to be peaceful on the one hand, but on the other not wanting to allow bigotry of any kind. It's a conflict in your soul.

meaningMnemonic: A leader stands upon the ground of the rice paddy . She is searching for treasure . It is said that this treasure here in this rice field will make things much easier for the leader (that's what leaders really want, after all). If she gets this treasure, it will be a great convenience for her, because convenience is everything when you're the leader. Hints Imagine the leader looking around the rice paddy. She keeps saying, "Ugh, it would be convenient if I didn't have to walk around out here looking for the treasure that's going to make things more convenient for me. Ugh." Go ahead and say this phrase out loud, too, pretending to be the leader in the rice paddy. Feel the cold and the wet, making it less convenient for you.
readingMnemonic: She finds a place to dig in the ground. It looks like there's some fresh dirt here. Finally, the treasure of convenience that will make this leader's life so much easier. She digs into the ground and pulls out a box. When she opens it, she finds out it's a ben to ( べん ). "My god," she thinks. "This really will make my life more convenient. My people can take their lunches with them now instead of coming back to base to eat, which will waste way less time!" Hints Feel the happiness that the leader would feel at this revelation. It will make everything much more convenient for her, since she's not the one doing all the manual labor. She won't have to eat out of a bento, that's for sure.

meaningMnemonic: By the time you finish digging a coffin hole with nothing but a spoon , you’ll be an old elderly person. Digging with nothing but a spoon takes a long time, especially when the hole needs to be big enough for a coffin. You might as well be digging it for yourself at this rate. By the time you finish, you’ll be all wrinkled and elderly and just about ready to keel over. Hints Imagine yourself digging a coffin hole with nothing but a spoon. Your hands get all cramped, your wrist starts to hurt, and you get painful blisters on your hands. It takes forever to dig a hole big enough for a coffin!
readingMnemonic: Now that you’re elderly (and probably about to die) you suddenly crave some delicious roe ( ろう ). Salmon roe, sea urchin roe, tofugu roe, doesn’t matter. Your old, tired bones need roe after all that hard work! Hints You hated roe when you were still young, but now that you’re an elderly old fart you really want to eat it. Roe is for old people, you guess, as you slurp it up.

meaningMnemonic: Orders coming from your mouth will determine the fate of your soldiers. You are their commanding officer and your orders determine their life and death. Hints Pretend you are a high ranking officer and imagine yourself giving orders to your underlings. Imagine all the power and influence you have. It feels good.
readingMnemonic: You are the commanding officer on the May flower ( めい ). You give orders to colonize America. The orders spewing from your mouth hole determine the fate of the settlers and the fate of America and the fate of the world! You and the Mayflower have changed everything forever. Hints Students of American history are very familiar with the Mayflower. Recall learning about it in school whenever you see this kanji. Or look it up on Wikipedia if you don’t know about it. The Mayflower is a big deal!

meaningMnemonic: Try to use your fingers to spoon out some of the sun and you'll come back with just one finger . Hints Look down at your finger and the burned stumps where the rest of your fingers used to be. It hurts. And you're sad. But at least you still have one finger left.
readingMnemonic: Don't worry, you aren't the only one out there with just one finger , shee p ( し ) only have one finger too. I mean, they're hooves, which are really just a single animal finger. It's just big and kind of flat. Hints Picture sitting with a sheep. It's right across from you, staring into your eyes. It reaches out its sheep finger hoof and you reach out with your finger. They touch. It's magical.

meaningMnemonic: You wear a special outfit and equip a sword whenever you do something for the first time. Doing something for the first time is always scary, but the right outfit and a sword at your side can give you the confidence and courage to overcome your jitters! Hints Imagine the butterflies in your stomach as you prepare to do something for the first time. Now look down at your badass outfit and the sword on your belt. Feel the nervousness subside a little. You've got this.
readingMnemonic: So, what is it you're doing for the first time? A fashion show ( しょ ). Your special outfit and sword aren't just to calm your nerves — they're also what you'll be showing off on the catwalk. Hints Picture yourself strutting down the runway at this fashion show. You're doing pretty well for your first show — until you trip over your sword and fall flat on your face. Darn it — now everyone's gonna know this was your first time.

meaningMnemonic: In your mouth there is a jet dropping flavor bombs. Every time you taste something, it's actually because a tiny jet has flown into your mouth to bomb you with flavor. Hints What's your favorite food? Imagine that, as you bite into it, tiny jets are released from inside the food to attack your tongue with flavor bombs, stimulating your sense of taste.
readingMnemonic: And what has more flavor than a big slab of me at ( み )? You love meat and its flavor nearly as much as you love the taste of its juice. So many good things to put in your mouth! Hints Of course, if you're vegetarian imagine the flavor of the meat being terrible. Up to you. Make the mnemonic work for your lifestyle.

meaningMnemonic: On a scooter there is a bear with a drop on its head trying to follow and chase you! You accidentally splashed it with water and it's not happy about it. You're on your own scooter, luckily, but that doesn't make this any less terrifying. Hints Picture the bear on its scooter with the offending drop of water on its head following really closely behind your scooter. You can almost feel his bear breath on your neck!
readingMnemonic: The bear is trying to follow you because it wants your o bi ( お ) as compensation for its injured pride. The obi is waving in the wind behind your scooter, and the bear is reaching out with its teeth to try and grab it. Hints Picture the bear chasing you on its scooter, trying to reach out and grab the obi off your waist. The drop of water on its head is jiggling from the exertion. Woah, it's getting a little too close!

meaningMnemonic: Your spirit should feel humble before a god 's spirit . You never really feel humble in front of anyone else, but if you meet a god's spirit… Well, you should probably lower yourself appropriately. Gods have powerful spirits. Hints Imagine a spirit appearing before you. It's a god. You should be as humble as possible. Out of respect and also because you don't want to be cursed or something.
readingMnemonic: When you meet a god 's spirit , you need to get down on your shin s ( しん ). Get down on your ankles? No, not low enough. Knees? No, no, get your shins flat on the ground to show how humble you really are. Luckily, you're wearing jean s ( じん ), so at least that will stop your poor shins getting chafed! Hints If you don't get down on your shins before god's spirit, it could take them away. Even your jeans couldn't protect you then. You don't want to live a shin-less life, do you?

meaningMnemonic: A drop of water to a root is good . It's good for the roots to grow and live and thrive. And what's good for roots is good for our plants and us humans too. Hints Imagine putting a little drop of water over a root you want to grow. Doing this is good for the plant and also good for your soul.
readingMnemonic: A good way to get a lot of drops of water for your roots is to buy a row boat ( りょう ). Then just row out to the middle of the lake and plonk all the roots right into the source! Hints Rowing even feels good on your arms and back. Probably just as good as all these roots will feel.

meaningMnemonic: The sound of your heart gives me an idea . The methodic thump thump thumping of a heart puts me in a trance that gives me great ideas. It’s a very inspirational sound, the sound of a heart is. It gives me an idea. Alternatively, you could look at this kanji and see a "stand" radical and something that kind of (almost) looks like the kanji for "think." When you stand up and think, you come up with your very own idea s! Hints Put your hand over your heart, or on your wrist, or somewhere you can feel your pulse. Your heart is pumping blood through your body, hear the sound of your heart beat and try to picture and get an idea for how all the blood flows through your body.
readingMnemonic: The heart of an ea gle ( い ) is very strong. The person who knew this probably came up with the idea to make the bald eagle a symbol of the United States. Eagles are always flying around and doing things, so their hearts are very strong. Hints Picture the majestic animal that is the bald eagle. Imagine the sound of an eagle screeching as it zooms through the air, flapping its wings in the wind. It’s pretty impressive.

meaningMnemonic: A Viking in a position of power does not need to labor in the fields. Labor is for the weak! A Viking of power takes what he wants, and need not labor for it. A powerful Viking plunders all and takes what he wants! Hints Imagine yourself as a powerful Viking. You have the power to take anything you want, pillaging and plundering to your heart’s content. Imagine all the things you would acquire with this sort of power. Note - there are a few other kanji that have a similar meaning to this one. This kanji is used in words related to physical, or manual labor, with an emphasis on how darn tiring it is!
readingMnemonic: It takes a lot of labor to harvest roe ( ろう ) so that’s what the Viking decides to take first! Roe is delicious, but it’s small and delicate. Vikings don’t labor for their own roe! They take it and eat it! Hints Picture this powerful Viking laying siege on a small fishing village and taking all the roe and stuffing it into his bearded face. So much labor went into harvesting that roe! Vikings are so mean!

meaningMnemonic: There are pieces of thread on each escalator showing you what level they go to in your school. Each escalator takes you to a different grade , so make sure you follow the right thread or you'll end up in a class that's either way above or way below your level. Hints When you level up your Japanese skills, you'll take this escalator to rank up too!
readingMnemonic: You want to see what the highest level is, so you go up the wrong escalator. At the top you find a giant cu cumber ( きゅう ). Hints A teacher comes over and says, "Excuse me, this is advanced level cucumber studies. I don't think you're at this level yet... please take the escalator down and follow the threads to find your level."

meaningMnemonic: There is a woman and a child in front of you. You like them very much. Hints Imagine a woman and a child you like very much. Just appreciate them, and think about how much you like those two. The reading mnemonic definitely won't ruin your image of them or anything.
readingMnemonic: "I like you two," you say to the woman and child. They both turn their heads 180 degrees back towards you. They both have faces that look just like こう いち 's. "We like you too," they say in unison. Hints And you DO like them. You have always been a fan of こういち 's kanji learning methods, and you feel so lucky to have married a woman who looks just like こういち and then (this is the real miracle!) gave birth to a child that looks like こういち too. Hashtag blessed.

meaningMnemonic: You've been playing blackjack in the sun since long ago . This is the longest game of blackjack you've ever played and it feels like ages since you started. You've been sitting out in the sun playing blackjack since long, long ago. Hints Imagine yourself playing a never-ending game of blackjack out in the hot sun. You’re sticky, sweaty, and tired. But all you can do is continue to play your game of blackjack. It’s miserable.
readingMnemonic: Once you finally finish the game, you walk the long walk back home, in the sun, barefoot, on a dirt road that hasn't been maintained since long ago . Your feet are all sweaty from being out in the sun, and walking on this dirt road gives you muck ashi ( むかし ). Your ashi (feet) are all mucky and muddy from the combination of dirt and sweat. Your muck ashi are really gross, man. Hints Imagine your muck ashi, all dirty and muddy from walking on that old road from long ago. Feel the muck between the toes of your ashi, squishing with every step. Hear the sound the mud makes as it slides between your sweaty mucky toes.

meaningMnemonic: The leader of your clan wants to live close to the ground so he demands you get low . Low, low, with your belly to the ground. That way you're always below him, since he's the leader. Hints Picture yourself, face smooshed into the ground, and you can hear the leader shouting above you, "GET LOW!"
readingMnemonic: Low people like you can only eat low food like potatoes. But that's boring, so you low people learned to make ta ter ( てい ) tots. You roll them to each other and eat them without lifting your heads. Hints Get low to the ground right now and ask your mom or dad to roll some tater tots towards your face. Eat them up, mm mm.

meaningMnemonic: Give trash to the moon and it will nurture and raise that trash like it's its own little moon baby. Hints Picture the moon raising this ball of trash, giving it love and attention.
readingMnemonic: The moon nurture s the trash ball until one day, it speaks! " 行く ( いく ), 行く！ " it says. It wants to go live with mom moon! Hints Watch as the little trash ball 行く s up into the sky and floats around its moon mama. If you raise your child right it will want to 行く wherever you go too.

meaningMnemonic: If you know the radical meaning orders you know the kanji meaning orders as well! Hints Here's an order: study your radicals.
readingMnemonic: Your orders are to get a ray ( れい ) gun. Hints Imagine an authority figure giving you this order as an official order. Ray guns don't really exist, so you think it's a pretty strange order. Hint: when you see the orders radical, the reading will often be れい . The mnemonic will likely involve orders to get a ray gun of some kind.

meaningMnemonic: Your fingers always seem to suit the random things you pick up off the ground. An old thimble. A discarded onion ring. A dead worm you tie in a knot. Your incredible fingers suit them beautifully, almost as if they were jewelry, so of course you pick up all of them. Hints Imagine finding something that suits your life and your style. You're not just going to leave it there, right? No, you're going to pick it up! Go on, use your fingers and pick up that thing.
readingMnemonic: You're walking around looking for something to pick up when you see a sword in a rock. Yes, this will suit you. You pick up the sword and people jump out around you and tell you that you are the new hero ( ひろ )! Uh oh. Maybe you shouldn't have picked this up. Hints You picked up the hero sword and now you're the new hero. Time to go kill a dragon. Good luck, and try not to die, hero person!

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami master has the power to pour water wherever he pleases. Tsunami masters are masters over the most powerful water force in the universe, so it makes sense that they have the ability to pour water at will, wherever they please. Best not tick off the master, unless you want a tsunami poured on your head. Hints Picture yourself as this tsunami master. You’re like a water bender from Avatar, only more awesome. Feel the cold wet water pouring out of your fingertips as you create water out of nothing. Imagine what it would be like to have this power.
readingMnemonic: If Chew bacca ( ちゅう ) was trying to attack you, you’d be able to defend yourself easily. Simply pour a tsunami on him and Chewbacca would surrender in a heartbeat. Chewbacca doesn’t like having water poured on him, especially not all the water from a tsunami. Hints Imagine Chewbacca soaking wet. All his fur is matted down and he looks pretty depressed. He smells like wet dog too. Smell this smell in your nostrils as you imagine how pathetic this drenched Chewbacca feels.

meaningMnemonic: Cut grain s with a knife to make them smaller and you'll make a great profit . By cutting them, now you can get three grains worth of money for what was once a single grain. Hints Imagine buying some rice. Now cut all the grains with a knife into smaller grains. Now sell them for two, three, four times the profit!
readingMnemonic: To make an even better profit , you decide to cut up ree ds ( り ) too. You stuff the grains in the reeds and sell that as "self-cooking" sets. Hints Picture all of your reeds full of grains in a row. The entire world will benefit from your crafty invention. And you'll turn a great profit too, which certainly doesn't hurt.

meaningMnemonic: A leader stand s at the highest rank in an organization. The leader is of the highest rank and stands above all others. Hints Picture this great leader. Imagine him actually standing on the shoulders of his supporters who are a lower rank than he is. He’s standing atop this great pyramid as a fearless leader.
readingMnemonic: This great leader is actually the leader of the boy scouts. And as we all know, the highest rank in boy scouts is the rank of ea gle ( い ) scout. This great leader has attained the rank of eagle scout and stands above all other scouts. Hints Picture the same ranking pyramid from before, only all the members are boy scouts, and the leader at the top is an eagle. Hear the piercing screech of the eagle with your ears.

meaningMnemonic: A leader who takes the middle of the road on every issue is likely to have an average relationship with everyone. He doesn't really take sides in matters, and just stays in the middle. This makes him seem like a wishy-washy people-pleaser, and as such he's only able to maintain average, mid-tier relationships. Hints I'm sure you've heard of flip-flopping in politics, when people try to take both sides of an issue, staying in the middle ground and never taking a stand. Imagine one of these people to represent this kanji.
readingMnemonic: Imagine a flip-flopping politician you have an average relationship with. Now imagine that there's a knocker ( なか ) on their forehead and you get to knock that knocker as hard as you like. Maybe you can knock some integrity into them and form a better relationship. Hints Also, this kanji is pronounced exactly like the vocab word 中 ( なか ). If you can remember that, it'll make remembering 仲 easier.

meaningMnemonic: As the year starts moving in the direction of winter , the trees must release their leaves. Hints Picture winter heading straight for you and frosting everything over. Now picture the leaves being released by the trees.
readingMnemonic: The trees release all of their leaves onto your ho me ( ほう ). Slowly, you watch in horror as your home is consumed by the released leaves. They enter in through the windows, doors, and the chimney. Hints "Release my home from this leaf prison!" you shout at the now bare trees.

meaningMnemonic: Grain s are few . Imagine the last few grains trickling down the hourglass. You only have a second left. Hints Normally an hourglass has sand to count the seconds, but yours uses grains. Imagine just a few grains left, and watch them trickle down as you count a second, and then another second.
readingMnemonic: After the final second s go by, your awful B.O. ( びょう ) appears. Hints Your hourglass timer was a timer to specifically let you know when your B.O. was set to return.

meaningMnemonic: Using your mouth , you smuggle into prison the parts necessary to make a crude knife . This gets you in trouble, and you wind up in a cell that's separate from everyone else. Hints Imagine how lonely and boring life is in your separate cell. You feel totally cut off and separated from the rest of the world.
readingMnemonic: Actually, another reason you wound up in a separate cell was because you were taking bets ( べつ ) from other inmates. Hints You took bets on all kinds of things: sports, jail yard fights, whether you could smuggle knife parts in your mouth, etc. Now you're stuck in your separate cell, paying the price for your actions. No more bets for you, buckaroo.

meaningMnemonic: The mountain on top of the cliff is dry unlike the shore below. Just from looking at the raging coast below, you'd think everything would be wet, it's splashing everywhere! Hints Imagine yourself on top of the mountain, looking down at the shore that stretches out below you. Notice how the coast extends as far as your eyes can see.
readingMnemonic: Sitting up there, watching the coast with you, is Gan dhi ( がん ). The world famous Gandhi, is just hanging out up here with you, looking down at what you now realize must be a coast in India. Hints Sit down next to Gandhi and close your eyes. You can hear the water hitting the shore below. The coastal birds are screaming. You crack open an eye and see Gandhi still sitting perfectly still.

meaningMnemonic: This cow temple is special . This cow must have been very important to have an entire temple dedicated to it. Hints Picture a temple dedicated to a single cow. All of the people who come and worship here have a special place in their hearts for the cow.
readingMnemonic: This cow is special because it belonged to Toku gawa ( とく ) Ieyasu, the first shōgun of the Tokugawa shogunate and uniter of Japan! He's a super important figure in Japanese history. You should absolutely look him up and read a bit about him (when you're caught up on these lessons, that is). Hints You walk up to a statue of the special cow in the temple and see a collar around its neck that says "Tokugawa Moo Moo" on it. How... special!

meaningMnemonic: The card game fish are best at is blackjack because they can easily hold the cards with their fins together . In blackjack you don't have to have a huge hand, full of cards. It's just a few, so fish fins can keep them together and just hit or stay. Hints Imagine a fish trying to hold a full hand of cards together. Impossible! Fish don’t have fingers to keep them spread properly. Now imagine a fish trying to hold two cards together and nodding to hit. It's much easier to keep things together this way!
readingMnemonic: Once a year trillions of fish get together in きょう と to play blackjack. They have a huge tournament there once a year. Hints Imagine a bunch of fish gathering together in きょうと to participate in this blackjack tournament. With so many fish all together in one place, it probably smells pretty fishy.

meaningMnemonic: A woman sits on a stool to conserve her power , as her servants toil away in the kitchen. They toil away preparing a feast for this powerful woman while she kicks back on her cozy stool. She's a queen and deserves to be pampered. Hints Imagine you're one of this woman's minions, toiling away in the kitchen. The heat from the stoves is intense, and you're hoping she doesn't see the sweat dripping from your forehead into the food. Man, you've never toiled so hard in your life. Note: There are a few other kanji with similar meanings. This one is used in words that refer to doing work, with a focus on making a concerted effort.
readingMnemonic: As a servant you toil not just for the woman, but also for her do g ( ど ). Anything she gets, the dog gets too. That means double the toil for you. But hey, at least the dog is cute. Hints Secretly it's this dog you toil for, not the woman. Try to picture what kind of dog it is. And imagine sneaking extra portions to it under the table when the woman isn't looking. Yes, if it weren't for this innocent dog, you'd have done with this life of toil!

meaningMnemonic: The leader has a cloud that he uses to transmit all of the messages he needs to send to his people. The cloud floats above him and when he wants to tell people something he just whispers into the cloud and it transmits his message really, really loudly to all of them. Hints Picture this special cloud floating above your leader. It's probably just a speaker attached to a drone covered in cotton balls.
readingMnemonic: As the leader transmit s his latest series of messages to you and the others, you notice a pretty large den t ( でん ) in it. That dent is probably a clue to what this cloud is really made of. Hints You highly doubt this is a magical cloud that can transmit messages. You inch closer to the big dent and try to poke it. Your finger goes right in! Hmm, you're still pretty sure there's a trick to this thing.

meaningMnemonic: A simple drunkard starting a war . Hints Imagine what the simple drunkard does, to start the war. They're not in their right mind, and the centaurs (getting you ready for the reading mnemonic!) are an easily offended people. Go ahead and run through the simple drunkard's actions toward the centaurs that start this war.

This kanji also means ocean , because presumably the people from the West, with their Western style, came from across the ocean. You'll want to be familiar with both meanings for vocab later on. Hints Imagine how ridiculous a sheep would look all decked out in Western-style cowboy gear. Now imagine it riding a tsunami wave as it screams, "Baa~ baa~ baa~!"
readingMnemonic: After a whole day of riding this tsunami, the sheep is hankerin' for some Western-style food, namely yo gurt ( よう ). Yogurt is Western-style food, right? If it helps you can imagine the yogurt is flavored like apple pie, to make it more American and Western. Hints Imagine yourself eating this Western-style apple pie yogurt. meaningMnemonic: Who will say turkey ? Who? WHO ??? Hints Say "who" over and over again, demanding someone says "turkey," for some reason.

This kanji is used in words that refer to doing work, with a focus on movement or operating something.
readingMnemonic: Where do you get the power to do all this work ? From dou ghnuts ( どう ). You eat nothing but doughnuts. If you had no doughnuts, you couldn't work. In fact, your leader pays you for your work… in doughnuts. Hints Picture yourself receiving a doughnut as payment after you've been working. It's delicious. Doughnuts are fantastic. readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: あの日、ここであなたと会えたのは運命ですよ。
sentences.english: It's destiny that I met you here on that day.

sentences.japanese: そういう運命だったんだよ。
sentences.english: It was meant to be like that.

sentences.japanese: iPhoneさん天国行き。用を足した後のトイレに落としちゃいました。まぁ、これがiPhoneさんの運命だったのかもしれないけどさ。でも、猛烈に悲しいぜよ...。
sentences.english: Rest in peace iPhone. I just dropped it in a toilet filled with more than just water. Maybe this was just fate but I am so sad right now.

meaningMnemonic: The energy you hold ( 持つ ) within you is your feeling s. What kind of feeling is your energy giving you today? 気持ち can refer to your current mood, to a particular emotion inside you, or to physical feelings and sensations. You hear it in phrases like 気持ちいい (feels good), 気持ちわるい (feels gross), or 気持ちが分かる (I understand how you feel).
readingMnemonic: 気 is on'yomi and you learned that with the kanji. 持ち , though, is kun'yomi, which you learned with the word 持つ . One of those weird exception readings, but the ち on the end of 持ち is a clue that it uses the kun'yomi.

sentences.english: there are feelings, to have feelings

sentences.japanese: あなたの気持ちはよく分かります。
sentences.english: I know exactly how you feel.

sentences.japanese: 朝起きた時から気持ちわるいんです。
sentences.english: I've been feeling sick since I woke up in the morning.

sentences.japanese: これ、つまらないものですが。ささやかな感謝の気持ちです。どうぞ、開けてみてください。
sentences.english: Here's a little something for you. This is just a small token of my appreciation. Go ahead, open it.

meaningMnemonic: When you have a "feeling" ( 気持ち ) that is "good" ( いい ), you are feeling good . 気持ちいい is what you say when something really feels good , both physically and emotionally. You can say it after stepping into a hot bath, feeling a cool breeze, or getting a massage that hits just right. It's the Japanese version of leaning back and going "ahhh, this feels nice!"
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from the vocab word 気持ち , so if you know that (or the vocab words 気 and 持つ ) you should be A-okay on this one. Feels good , right?

sentences.japanese: マッサージは気持ちいい
ジョギングは気持ちいい
おひさまが気持ちいい
エアコンが気持ちいい
このブランケット、気持ちいい。
家がきれいだと気持ちいいよね！
sentences.english: Doesn't it feel good to have a clean house?

sentences.japanese: マッサージ中、気持ち良すぎてイビキをかいてたみたい。
sentences.english: It looks like I felt so comfortable that I was snoring during the massage.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are almost exactly the same. The only difference is that this word can mean finger or toe . What are toes but small, walking fingers?
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember: What do you use your finger for the most? For pointing, of course! Imagine going up to people and saying, "What will you be ( ゆび ) when you grow up?" Point your finger at the next person, "What will you be?" Keep going until you're just saying, "You be? You be?" with your finger out.

sentences.japanese: なんで手の指も足の指も五本なんだろう？
sentences.english: Why do we have five fingers and also five toes?

sentences.japanese: 中指がいきなりいたくなったんだけど。
sentences.english: My middle finger just started hurting all of a sudden.

sentences.japanese: 指切りしたんだから、わすれないでね！
sentences.english: We pinky promised, so don't forget!

meaningMnemonic: When you are number one in rank , you're in first place .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 一位になったら、一週間毎日カレーを作ってあげる。
sentences.english: If you get first place, I'll make you curry every day for a week.

sentences.japanese: 妹がピアノコンクールで一位をとりました。
sentences.english: My sister took first place in the piano competition.

sentences.japanese: お母さん！僕、あのテストで滅茶苦茶良い点をとったんだよ！なんとクラスで一位だったんだ！
sentences.english: Mom! I really aced that test! I ranked at the top of my class!

meaningMnemonic: If you're at neck rank you're in first place . Haven't you ever heard the phrase, "neck and neck" when two people in a race are both super close to first place? Just remember that and you'll never forget this word.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You learned this reading for 首 when you learned 部首 , and the reading for 位 is the one you learned with the kanji, so you should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.english: to hold on to first place

sentences.japanese: 学力テストで首位に立った。
sentences.english: I got the first place in an academic test.

sentences.japanese: あの女の人は世界ランキング首位のテニスプレーヤーです。
sentences.english: That woman is the world's top ranked tennis player.

sentences.japanese: その老人は、両チームの首位争いには全く興味が無いようだった。
sentences.english: That old person seemed to have zero interest in both teams' fight for first place.

meaningMnemonic: Long ago people used to talk about all sorts of things. Most of them weren't true. Long ago people liked to lie a lot. Now we call those things they talked about folk tale s and legend s.
readingMnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You learned them both already, so you should be able to read this on your own. Just watch out for the rendaku of はなし to ばなし .

sentences.english: to tell an old story, to reminisce

sentences.japanese: これは日本の昔話ですか。
sentences.english: Is this a Japanese folk tale?

sentences.japanese: まるで昔話の中に出てくるプリンセスみたいね。
sentences.english: You're like a princess that appears in an old tale.

sentences.japanese: バス待合所でバスを待ちながら、昔話の絵本を子どもに読み聞かせた。
sentences.english: While waiting for a bus in the bus shelter, I read a folk tale picture book for my child.

meaningMnemonic: An eat thing (aka "a thing you eat") is food . Eat those things. Eat that food. Because it's a "thing" you know it's a noun. Interesting how this kanji can turn a verb like this into a noun, right? Look out for it because this pattern will show up with other verbs as well!
readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, but you know them both now, so you should be able to read this too!

sentences.japanese: 安田さんは、食べ物をおねがいします。
sentences.english: Please bring some food, Ms. Yasuda.

sentences.japanese: これは本当に食べ物ですか？石みたいですが。
sentences.english: Is this really food? It looks like a stone.

sentences.japanese: 食べ物を粗末にするとバチが当たりますよ。
sentences.english: When you waste food, heaven will punish you.

meaningMnemonic: If you have a friend you like , well, that's true friendship !
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: このキーホルダーは、私たちの友好のシンボルです。
sentences.english: This key chain is a sign of our friendship.

sentences.japanese: 日本と米国の友好は強いですか？
sentences.english: Is the friendship between Japan and the United States strong?

sentences.japanese: あそこの家のおじさん友好的だけど、実はヤクザの隠れメンバーらしいよ！
sentences.english: The man who lives in that house over there is friendly, but apparently he's secretly a yakuza member!

meaningMnemonic: When you return the doing s of another person, you're doing it to get even (whether it's a nice thing or a mean thing).
readingMnemonic: The readings are a bit weird, here. 仕 gets its on'yomi reading... you should be okay with that. 返し gets the kun'yomi reading, though, which is the reading you saw with the word 返す in level 9. You can tell this part uses the kun'yomi vocab reading because it has that hiragana attached to it. Just remember to distinguish between the two parts of the word to remember the readings.

sentences.japanese: ムカつくから、なんか仕返ししたいな。
sentences.english: I find it quite annoying, so I wanna get even.

sentences.japanese: 本当に最低の女！いつか仕返ししてやるわ！
sentences.english: Seriously, she is the worst! I'll get even with her someday!

sentences.japanese: プリンを食べられた仕返しに、コウイチの好きなヨーグルトを食べてやった。
sentences.english: To get back at him for eating my pudding, I ate Koichi's favorite yogurt.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: Do you know the word "Kamikaze"? Also, do you remember the word 風 from a previous level? Kamikaze means "divine winds" or "godly winds." If you know the word "Kamikaze" you can apply it to this single word, that means "god" or "gods." Use your prior knowledge to remember this reading.

sentences.english: child of god, the Son of God (Christianity)
to offer to god, to devote to god

sentences.japanese: 神はどこかにいると思いますか？
sentences.english: Do you think the gods exist somewhere?

sentences.japanese: 神に相談できるコールセンターがあったら良いのに。
sentences.english: I wish there were a call center where I could consult with God.

sentences.japanese: 神様は水の上を歩けるかもしれないけど、俺は草地の上を泳ぐことができるんだぜ。
sentences.english: God may be able to walk on water, but I can swim in the meadow.

meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of good ? It's also good .
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember: A good way to pass the time is with a yo -yo ( よ ). But it better be a good yo-yo. A bad one will just fall apart. Note that よい is a more formal or literary way of saying "good," the more common one being いい . To distinguish the different readings, the latter version is usually written in just kana too!

sentences.japanese: そのアイディアすごい良いですね！
sentences.english: I think that idea is very good!

sentences.japanese: ケンカするほど仲が良いって言うだろ？
sentences.english: You say you're getting along well as you fight, right?

sentences.japanese: 良い考えだけど、実際それをするには資金が足りないんだよね。
sentences.english: It's a good idea, but we don't have enough money to do it.

meaningMnemonic: You toil and use your strength . Ugh! How difficult. You really put in a great effort .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: to continue one’s efforts, to keep trying
the efforts of the person in question

sentences.japanese: あんた、努力しないで社長になれるとでも思ってんの？
sentences.english: Hey, are you really thinking you can become a company president without making any efforts?

sentences.japanese: 宝くじを当てるのだって、それなりの努力が必要なんだよ！
sentences.english: Even winning the lottery requires a certain amount of effort, alright?

sentences.japanese: 意味のない努力？そんなものないよ。
sentences.english: Meaningless effort? There's no such thing.

meaningMnemonic: Suffering and labor . Sounds like the kind of thing these soft hands wouldn't want to deal with. These are hardships and troubles . Hopefully you don't have too much of this with kanji anymore!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: to cause someone trouble, to cause someone anxiety

sentences.japanese: ワニカニに出会うまでは、おれの人生は苦労ばかりだった。
sentences.english: My life was full of hardships until I came across WaniKani.

sentences.japanese: このコウイチのサイン、苦労してやっと手に入れたんだよ。
sentences.english: I went through hardship to finally get Koichi's autograph.

sentences.japanese: うちのお風呂って、シャワーの位置が固定されちゃってるから、バスタブを洗って流すときにかなり苦労するんだよね。
sentences.english: In my bathtub, the position of the shower is fixed, so it is quite difficult to wash and rinse.

meaningMnemonic: A "suffering hand" is a little misleading. Think more in terms of the words 苦い (bitter) and 手 (person... remember how that happens sometimes?). Now think of this word like you're bitter about having to work with someone. Why? Because they are extremely hard to deal with .
readingMnemonic: The reading is that of 苦い ( にがい ) plus regular old 手 ( て ). Remember, this is your bitter person, the person who's "hard to deal with." So, it uses the strange にがい reading.

sentences.japanese: コミュニケーションが苦手

sentences.english: things one is not good at
someone who is hard to deal with, people who are not good at something
to become bad at, to come to dislike
to consider to be a weak point
to look like one is not good at something
I'm not a big fan of celery.

sentences.japanese: あのアイドル、歌が苦手なのが欠点なんだよな。
sentences.english: The drawback about that idol is that she is not a good singer.

sentences.japanese: うちの犬がなんでお前にばっかり吠えるかって？たぶん、お前のことが苦手なんだよ。
sentences.english: Why does my dog bark only at you? He probably just doesn't like you.

meaningMnemonic: A tall grade item is really just a high grade or high-class item.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: こんな高級なプレゼントもらえません。
sentences.english: I can't accept such a high-class gift.

sentences.japanese: これは中国で有名な高級茶なんですよ。
sentences.english: This is a famous high-end tea in China.

sentences.japanese: あの高級レストランはVIP専用で、入店には招待状か紹介状が必要なんだって。
sentences.english: That luxury restaurant is exclusive for VIPs, and to enter, you'll need an invitation or a referral.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how you learned that 仮名 means "kana?" Well this is flat kana. Flat kana is just hiragana .
readingMnemonic: You should know the reading for this word because it's the same as the English meaning.

sentences.japanese: うちの子には平仮名の名前をつけたいんです。
sentences.english: I want to name my child with hiragana.

sentences.japanese: このチョコレートを食べると平仮名を全部おぼえることができますよ。
sentences.english: If you eat this chocolate, you can memorize all of the hiragana.

meaningMnemonic: You know that the kanji 付 means attach and words like 付く mean "to be attached." This has the same idea. When you see this attached to another word, for example, you might know that something is attached to something else, or perhaps included with it. For example, if you stay at a hotel room, maybe it is a breakfast 付き , i.e. " including breakfast."
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from the reading of the kanji as well as from words like 付く and 付ける .

sentences.japanese: このスプーンはケース付きですよ。
sentences.english: These spoons come with a case.

sentences.japanese: この辺にプール付きのホテルはありますか？
sentences.english: Is there a hotel with a pool around here?

sentences.japanese: この部屋は冷蔵庫、洗濯機付きです。
sentences.english: This room is furnished with a refrigerator and a washing machine.

meaningMnemonic: Something that is not convenience is inconvenient .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: この辺りでは、車を持っていないとかなり不便ですよ。
sentences.english: Not having a car around here is really inconvenient.

sentences.japanese: もし不便なことがあればすぐにフロントデスクに言ってくださいね。
sentences.english: If there is any inconvenience, let the front desk know immediately.

sentences.japanese: 俺の隠れ家へようこそ。ビールは冷蔵庫に入ってるぜ。ちょっと不便かもしれねぇが、煙草は外で吸ってくれよな。
sentences.english: Welcome to my man cave. Beers are in the refrigerator. It may be a bit inconvenient for you, but you’ve got to go outside to smoke.

meaningMnemonic: Something at the middle level or grade is at an intermediate level .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 中級とは、どういったレベルですか？
sentences.english: What kind of level is an intermediate level?

sentences.japanese: 中級の日本語クラスに入りたいんです。
sentences.english: I want to join the intermediate Japanese class.

sentences.japanese: この会社には英語が中級の人たちは少ない。
sentences.english: There are only a few people who are intermediate English speakers at this company.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 始める means "to begin something"? 始め is its noun version and means "beginning," as in the start of an action or process. に marks a point in time. So 始めに means in the beginning . 始めに can also mean to begin with or to start with when introducing an opening action, like 始めに、ウォーミングアップをしましょう (let's begin with some warm-up exercises).
readingMnemonic: The reading is kun'yomi (look at all that hiragana!) but that's the reading you learned with the word 始める , so have no fear, you got it!

sentences.japanese: 始めに、プレゼンテーションをしたいと思います。
sentences.english: First, I'd like to make a presentation.

sentences.japanese: 始めにキャベツを切ります。
今年の仕事始めにはパスタを食べました。
sentences.english: I ate pasta on my first day of work this year.

meaningMnemonic: You know 事 means "occurrence," but it can also mean "thing." So when you're doing thing s all day, what are you probably doing? A job ! All jobs really just amount to doing things. Just like "job" in English, 仕事 can refer to a person's specific occupation , to work in general, or to a particular task depending on the context.
readingMnemonic: This word uses the on'yomi reading for 仕 and the kun'yomi reading for 事 . Please note that 事 uses the reading こと , which you didn't learn with the kanji, but you have come across it once or twice by now, and because of the way rendaku works, it's changed to the voiced ごと .

sentences.japanese: 新しい仕事を始めてから、まだ三日です。
sentences.english: Since I started a new job, it has only been three days.

sentences.japanese: 今日は六時まで仕事が終わらないから、それまで近くのカフェにいてね。
sentences.english: I won't be able to sign off work until six o'clock today, so stay in a nearby cafe until then.

sentences.japanese: 赤ちゃんの仕事は泣くことです。
sentences.english: The baby's job is to cry.

meaningMnemonic: If people work together on the same thing, they're working on a joint project. They're doing something collaborative . 共同 is used when two or more people or groups do something together with a shared purpose or responsibility. 共同作業 (collaborative work) means you share tasks with others, for example, and 共同生活 (shared living) means living together with someone, whether it's a partner or a roommate.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: チームメイトとの共同作業は楽しいです。
sentences.english: Collaborative tasks with teammates are fun.

sentences.japanese: ここは学生の共同コーワーキングスペースです。
sentences.english: This is a co-working space for students to share.

sentences.japanese: これは日本とアメリカのチームが共同開発したトイレです。
sentences.english: This is a toilet jointly developed by teams from Japan and the United States.

meaningMnemonic: Something happened direct ly before this. In other words, it happened just before this. 直前 is used to talk about something happening immediately prior to something else, like when your date cancels on you just before you were supposed to meet or your doctor tells you not to eat a snack right before bed.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 出発の直前に雨がふりだした。
sentences.english: It started raining right before we left.

sentences.japanese: ゴール直前でこけてしまった。
sentences.english: I fell down right before the goal.

sentences.japanese: 直前のキャンセルだったので、お金はほとんどもどってこなかった。
sentences.english: Because it was a last-minute cancellation, I hardly got any money back.

sentences.japanese: すしを食べる直前にしょうゆがないと気づいたんです。
sentences.english: Just as I was about to eat sushi, I realized there was no soy sauce.

meaningMnemonic: If 丁度 is "exactly", then "exactly good" is going to be just the right amount, aka just right .
readingMnemonic: If you know the reading for 丁度 you'll know the reading for this too. Your knowledge should be just right , as they say inside my head.

sentences.japanese: 大きすぎず、小さすぎず、本当に丁度いいサイズです。
sentences.english: It's not too big or too small. It's just the right size.

sentences.japanese: あっ、丁度いいところに来たね！
sentences.english: Oh, you came at the right time!

sentences.japanese: このぐらいの温度が丁度いいですね。

meaningMnemonic: Someone who does labor for work is a laborer .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: コウイチ社長は、日本の労働者不足についてどうお考えなんですか？
sentences.english: What does president Koichi think about the shortage of workers in Japan?

sentences.japanese: 私たちのような労働者たちがこの国を支えてるんですよ。
sentences.english: Workers like us are supporting this country.

sentences.japanese: 社長という立場なら、労働者の権利を守ってくださいよ。
sentences.english: If you are a president, please try to protect the rights of workers.

meaningMnemonic: A vocab made from a single kanji all alone usually keeps at least one of the meanings of its kanji parent. In this case, that's life .
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: The Book of Enoch ( いのち ) has passed down your fate and told you how to use your life . You must read the book of Enoch and find out what you're supposed to do.

sentences.japanese: 虫の命だって、大切な命なんだよ。
sentences.english: Even a bug's life is an important life.

sentences.japanese: このフィギュアは命の次に大切なんです。
sentences.english: This figure is the second most important thing, after my life.

sentences.japanese: このレスキュー船には、たくさんの人の命がかかっています。
sentences.english: Many people's lives depend on this rescue ship.

sentences.japanese: 神様、お願いです。私の命と引き換えに、この子の命を助けてください。
sentences.english: God, please. Save this child's life in exchange for my own.

meaningMnemonic: You know that 好 means like and this vocab word means the same thing: like or love ! This word is an adjective in Japanese, so a more literal translation is likable or lovable . Still, it usually sounds more natural to translate it as a verb in English.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Who do you like more than anyone? Your friend Sue . If you know someone named Sue, pretend you like her. If you don't, think of a famous person you know named Sue and use her, pretending you're good friends that like each other a lot.

sentences.english: to come to like, to fall in love
to like one's job, to like work

meaningMnemonic: If someone asks if you want a separate knee ( に ), you'll say not particularly . I mean, you've never thought about it, but do you really need more knees? Not really ... In this first meaning, 別に is often used on its own, or with a negative verb or adjective, as in 別に長くない (not particularly long). However, when 別に is used with a positive verb, it often simply means separately , or in addition to . After all, when you have to do something separately, you have to do it in addition to something else. Like learning this meaning in addition to the first one. What a chore!

meaningMnemonic: The place where they accept paperwork and attach stuff to it is reception . Hand them your forms, and they'll be covered with sticky notes and paperclips before you know it. 受付 is where things officially get received, checked in, or processed at a business, institution, or event. It can refer to the reception desk itself, the receptionist behind it, or even the procedures that get handled there, as in 受付番号 (application number, reception number) or 受付をすませる (finish check-in or registration). Note that it can also be written as 受け付け , since it originally comes from combining 受ける (to receive something) and 付ける (to attach something).

readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, but you know them both now, so you should be able to read this too! One hint that this is a kun'yomi reading word is the hiragana in the center. It's like two separate words combined together, and when a word is a single kanji / a single kanji with hiragana attached it is usually kun'yomi. This is like two of those, combined.

meaningMnemonic: You know 別 means separate , and the の here shows it's being used as an adjective to describe something. So it's like saying "a separate ______," "a different ______," or " another ______."
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned. Move on to a 別の漢字 , ok?

meaningMnemonic: When you say separate separate , you're putting things off into their own areas. So 別々 means separate . Note that this word is typically used in reference to multiple separate items, as opposed to 別の , which refers to a single separate or different thing. It's also used a lot as an adverb with the particle に to mean "separately."
readingMnemonic: The reading is just the べつ reading you know, twice.

meaningMnemonic: The way / road of the god (s) is, as you can probably guess, a big Japanese religion. There's two, and I'll give you a hint, this one isn't Buddhism (that would probably have the kanji for Buddha in it, no?). So what's the other big one? It's Shinto . If you're having trouble remembering this because you've never heard of it before, skip to the reading. The reading will help.
readingMnemonic: The reading is a bit wonky. 神 should be no problem. 道 on the other hand is almost the one you learned ( どう ) but now it's とう for some reason. Perhaps the gods took away the dakuten to make it とう , who knows. All I know is that it's best not to question said gods. If you already know of Shinto in English, though, this reading should be really easy. If you don't, perhaps you can use this reading to help you to remember Shinto the religion.

sentences.japanese: 神道には特に教えがないんですよ。

meaningMnemonic: A God company ... think of this as "what 'company' does the god's work?" Well, the answer to that is a shrine, probably. In this case a Shinto shrine because of the しん in 神 .
readingMnemonic: But wait! 神 is read じん in this word for some reason. Darn those gods, always messing around, adding dakuten. Maybe this will help, though: Imagine yourself at a Shinto shrine. You are praying to the gods, asking for food. Out from the sky rains ginger ( じんじゃ ). You are pelted with it and not sure if you should be happy or upset.

to be at the shinto shrine
to be at the shinto shrine
in front of the shinto shrine

meaningMnemonic: You've hopefully seen 買う by now and know it means "to buy." So, 買い is going to be similar to that. Add that to thing and you have a "buying things" sort of word. What does "buying things" describe? It describes shopping .
readingMnemonic: The readings are the kun'yomi, which is usually the case when there's hiragana in the middle. You learned the reading for 買い when you learned the kanji, as well as the word 買う , and you learned this reading of 物 in the word 物 !

meaningMnemonic: One of the kanji meanings is side , and as a standalone word this also means side , as in the sides of a shape.
readingMnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

meaningMnemonic: If you try to see a bunch of thing s at once, you are probably sightseeing or watching . This can also refer to the person doing the action, so it can sometimes mean sightseer too.
readingMnemonic: The reading is all on'yomi, and you know how to read 物 . 見 's on'yomi ( けん ) is a reading you didn't learn with the kanji because it's so much less useful, but you do have to know it here. You've seen it with 発見 a couple levels ago, so that should help. Just imagine taking the samurai Ken on an epic sightseeing trip. Think of all the things you and Ken will visit!

meaningMnemonic: When the sell ing is cut , that means something is sold out . You'll see this word a lot in stores (or, hopefully you won't...) in Japan. Look out for it if you're able!
readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, but you know them both now, so you should be able to read this too!

sentences.english: This book was sold out for a long time, but it finally came back in stock!

meaningMnemonic: You know the single word 時 , right? It means time . This is that twice. So you have one time, and you have another time. They are separate. Things don't happen in every of these times you have. They happen sometimes .
readingMnemonic: The reading is the vocab word 時 twice, with the second one getting rendaku'd.

meaningMnemonic: Something that is special and separate from the rest is, well, special .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

社長がわざわざオフィスに来たなんて何か特別なミーティングでもあったんですか？
sentences.english: Was there a special meeting or something that the president bothered to come all the way to the office for?

meaningMnemonic: Learner, if you see a thing , then it must be splendid . You saw it, after all, so of course it's magnificent . You only see the beautiful things in this world. And that's an admirable quality.
readingMnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You learned them already, so you should be able to read this on your own. Just remember that there is rendaku on こと and it becomes ごと .

meaningMnemonic: A language about thing s. This is a confusing one. Just think of it more like someone talking about things, anything, really. Someone who just talks about things is someone who tells stories. So, this word means tale or story or legend (not the Tom Cruise one, though).
readingMnemonic: Both kanji take the kun'yomi here. For 物 , that's もの , which you learned with the vocabulary 物 . You learned the kun'yomi for 語 with the verb 語る , but here it becomes がたり because of rendaku, and the り is tucked inside the kanji. Maybe you've already heard the word ものがたり too. It's in some film and book names. If you haven't, and you find this reading hard to remember, think of a story about an infamous Gatling ( がたり ) gun that wandered the land, mowing everything down in its path. It's a terrible legend, but what if it were true???

アンデルセン物語を読んであげましょう。

It's the same kind of "West" that people mean when they talk about Western culture and all that.

You haven't learned this reading yet for 西 ( せい ), so here's a mnemonic to help you out: People are attacking from the West , so you pull out your sa ber ( せい ) and beat them back. You keep pushing further and further west until you reach the ocean and there's nowhere left for them to run. Your saber saves the day! Take that, the West.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means advance , and this verb means to advance something or to move something forward . This is a transitive verb, so you act upon something else. You advance something. You move something forward. Like a school project, or your plans for taking over the world.
readingMnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn with the kanji. Here's a mnemonic to help: You are moving your lawsuit forward against Sue. But now she says that YOU'RE the problem. " Sue, sue me ," ( すすめ ) you say as you continue to advance the lawsuit. Make sure to say "me" like "mehh," in a really snobbish way.

sentences.japanese: どうぞ、インタビューを進めて下さい。
この雪じゃ、これ以上工事を進められないよ。

meaningMnemonic: When you determine and use your finger to point at someone or something, you're going to appoint them. The する on the end makes it a verb, so 指定 would be "appointment" or "designation" or something along those lines. Cool how する works.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means become so the vocab verb version would be to become . While the kanji version is worth knowing, be aware that you'll usually see this verb written in hiragana.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You are starting to become something else. You're transforming, but you're not sure into what. First, you get fins... Uh oh, something in the water. Then, you gain a tail and rubbery skin... Hmm, something sea mammal-like. Oh, and then a huge horn sprouts out of your face. You are going to become a na rwhal ( な ).

sentences.english: to be much obliged to someone, to be indebted to someone

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means raise so the verb vocab version means to be raised . P.S. This word is for when you are being raised, not when you are doing the raising of someone. That's 育てる . You'll learn it later.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: When you were raised, you were raised completely on soda ( そだ ). That's all you drank. No water, no juice... just tons and tons of soda. Imagine this.

sentences.english: I was born and raised in Tokyo.

sentences.english: Love grew between the dog and Koichi.

meaningMnemonic: You hopefully know the word 返す , which means "to return" (as in, you're doing the direct action of returning something). This word, on the other hand, is the version where something just returns (and you're not doing the action of returning it). Use the る to help you to remember this. る the Kangaroo is returned to you. You don't do any of the returning, it just happens or someone else does it. That's why this word means to be returned . Note this word is often combined with くる (to come), which reinforces the aspect that something is coming back to you.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as 返す , so as long as you know that you'll be able to apply it here to learn the reading of this word as well.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means compare so the verb vocab version is to compare .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. sentences.english: Air transmits sound to our ears.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 欠 means lack ? This verb is related. The 欠かす form is a little tricky, but it's sort of like you're causing yourself to lack something. So it means to do without . Just keep in mind this word is most often used in the negative, like 欠かせないもの (things you can't do without) or 朝のコーヒーは欠かさない (never go without morning coffee). You can remember 欠かす this way: Since you cause yourself to lack something with this word, it's all your fault. That's why you want to cuss ( かす ). You made yourself miss out on something. meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means follow so the verb version is to follow (it's also to chase , because when you follow something you are chasing it too).
